title: Warner sued Suno. Now it takes a cut. Who else gets paid?
subtitle: Warner, BMG and Believe now get a share of Suno's revenue. Universal and Sony sue it again. Here is who gets paid when a fan makes a song with AI.

images.label: Who gets paid when a fan makes a song with AI
images.alt: The money path: 1, the fan pays Suno, because downloading needs a paid account; 2, Suno collects, then passes on a portion; 3, Warner, BMG and Believe get a share from launch day. Past the labels, it goes dark: 4, the artist's share is set by label contracts nobody has published. Sony and Universal are still suing.
images.caption: "A portion": Jack Brody, Suno's chief product officer, to Music Business Worldwide (MBW)

images.label: Same app, same songs, two opposite bets
images.alt: Two camps. Partners: Warner settled and became Suno's partner in November 2025; from 9 September 2026 Warner, BMG and Believe get a share of Suno's revenue. Suing: Sony and Universal sued Suno over 560 recordings in June 2024, still running, and sued again over 60,202 recordings on 18 September 2026. While suing Suno, Universal signed AI deals with Udio in October 2025 and ElevenLabs on 10 September 2026.
images.caption: Sources: Warner Music Group, Suno, Universal Music Group and ElevenLabs announcements; the labels' complaints, as reported by MBW

images.label: How these fights ended, and our call
images.alt: Warner's suit against Suno ended in a partnership. Universal's fight with Udio ended in licences. Our call, 70% sure: by 31 December 2027, Universal or Sony will have announced a settlement or a licensing deal with Suno. Why both sides want a deal: Suno faces a theoretical ceiling of just over $9 billion in the new suit alone; the labels risk a judge calling training fair use.
images.caption: Just over $9 billion is MBW's theoretical maximum for the new suit, at the top rate of $150,000 a work. The judge picks where to land.
